title: Angle chasing and polygons
blurb: How to find angles quickly using parallel lines, isosceles triangles, polygon angle sums and the basic circle theorems.
outcomes: Chase angles through parallel lines and isosceles triangles, naming one unknown when stuck
Use polygon angle sums and the angle at the centre theorem with its consequences
Spot hidden circles and use the circumcircle of a regular polygon to read off angles
lesson:
In triangle $ABC$ the angle at $A$ is $50^\circ$, and the bisectors of the angles at $B$ and $C$ meet at $I$. What is $\angle BIC$?

We are not told $\angle B$ or $\angle C$, and they cannot be found, so call them $2b$ and $2c$. The angle sum of $ABC$ gives $2b + 2c = 130^\circ$, so $b + c = 65^\circ$. In triangle $BIC$ the angles at $B$ and $C$ are $b$ and $c$, so $\angle BIC = 180^\circ - 65^\circ = 115^\circ$. Note that $b$ and $c$ were never found; only $b + c$ was needed. The same argument shows $\angle BIC = 90^\circ + \tfrac12\angle A$ for every triangle.

This is angle chasing: name the unknown angles, apply the basic facts, and continue until one angle has been written in two ways. This unit collects the facts you need.

Basic facts

Angles on a straight line add to $180^\circ$, angles round a point add to $360^\circ$, and vertically opposite angles are equal. When a line crosses two parallel lines, alternate angles (the Z shape) are equal, corresponding angles (the F shape) are equal, and co-interior angles (the C shape) add to $180^\circ$. Each of these also works backwards: if alternate angles are equal, the lines are parallel.

Triangle facts. The angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$. The exterior angle at one vertex equals the sum of the interior angles at the other two vertices.

To see why, draw the line through $A$ parallel to $BC$. It makes alternate angles equal to $\angle B$ and $\angle C$ with $AB$ and $AC$, and together with $\angle A$ these fill a straight line. The exterior angle at $C$ is $180^\circ - \angle C$, which is therefore $\angle A + \angle B$. Use the exterior angle fact directly, rather than going through the angle sum.

Isosceles triangles

If two sides of a triangle are equal, the angles opposite them are equal, and conversely. If the apex angle is $\theta$, each base angle is $90^\circ - \tfrac12\theta$. Most contest angle problems depend on isosceles triangles, so the first thing to do with any diagram is to look for equal lengths. They come from three places: lengths you are told are equal, sides of regular polygons (and of the squares and equilateral triangles attached to them), and radii of a circle.

When a problem only says that an isosceles triangle has an angle of $40^\circ$, there are two triangles: $40^\circ, 70^\circ, 70^\circ$ and $40^\circ, 40^\circ, 100^\circ$. Check both.

Polygons

Polygon angles. The interior angles of a convex $n$-sided polygon add to $(n-2)\times 180^\circ$, and its exterior angles add to $360^\circ$. So each interior angle of a regular $n$-gon is $180^\circ - \dfrac{360^\circ}{n}$.

For the first fact, join one vertex to every other vertex: this cuts the polygon into $n-2$ triangles, and their angles together make up the interior angles. For the second, walk round the boundary. At each corner you turn through the exterior angle, and after one lap you face the way you started, having made one full turn. Know the regular values: $60^\circ, 90^\circ, 108^\circ, 120^\circ, 135^\circ, 140^\circ, 144^\circ, 150^\circ$ for $n = 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12$.

Circle theorems

Angle at the centre. If $A$, $B$, $C$ lie on a circle with centre $O$, and $C$ is on the major arc $AB$, then $\angle AOB = 2\angle ACB$.

Draw the diameter $CD$. Since $OA = OC$, triangle $OAC$ is isosceles, so if $\angle OCA = x$ then $\angle OAC = x$ as well, and the exterior angle $\angle AOD$ equals $2x$. In the same way $\angle OCB = y$ gives $\angle DOB = 2y$. Adding, $\angle AOB = 2x + 2y = 2\angle ACB$. If $O$ happens to lie outside triangle $ABC$, subtract instead of adding and the same argument works.

The other standard facts follow from this, with one extra fact needed for tangents.

  • Same segment. Angles standing on the same chord, on the same side of it, are equal: each is half the same angle at the centre.
  • Semicircle. The angle in a semicircle is $90^\circ$, because the angle at the centre is a straight angle.
  • Cyclic quadrilateral. Opposite angles add to $180^\circ$, because the two angles at the centre make a full turn.
  • Tangents. A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at its point of contact. The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the opposite segment (the alternate segment theorem): if $AD$ is the diameter from the point of contact $A$, both angles equal $90^\circ - \angle BAD$, where $B$ is the other end of the chord.

Regular polygons are cyclic. The vertices of a regular $n$-gon lie on a circle, and each side subtends $\dfrac{360^\circ}{n}$ at the centre. So each side subtends $\dfrac{180^\circ}{n}$ at every other vertex, and any angle formed by three vertices is $\dfrac{180^\circ}{n}$ times the number of sides on the arc it stands on.

The method

To chase angles, we have the following method. Mark every angle you know on the diagram. Look for equal lengths before anything else and mark the isosceles triangles they create. If you get stuck, call one well-chosen angle $x$ (usually the one everything else depends on) and write the other angles in terms of it. You are finished when one angle has been expressed in two different ways. If three equal lengths come out of one point, draw the circle they define.

Example 1. Lines $\ell$ and $m$ are parallel. A path goes from $A$ on $\ell$ to $P$, then to $Q$, then to $B$ on $m$, as shown. The angle between $\ell$ and $AP$ is $38^\circ$, $\angle APQ = 74^\circ$, and the angle between $QB$ and $m$ is $27^\circ$. Find $x = \angle PQB$.

We could extend $AP$ to meet $m$ and look for triangles, but the only facts that connect angles at different points here are the parallel line facts. So draw the dashed lines through $P$ and $Q$ parallel to $\ell$ (one parallel through each bend).

The dashed line through $P$ splits the $74^\circ$ angle into two parts. The upper part and the $38^\circ$ angle at $A$ are alternate angles between parallel lines, so the upper part is $38^\circ$ and the lower part is $74^\circ - 38^\circ = 36^\circ$. At $Q$ the dashed line splits $x$ into two parts. The upper part is alternate to that $36^\circ$ (the segment $PQ$ crosses two parallel lines), and the lower part is alternate to the $27^\circ$ at $B$. So $x = 36^\circ + 27^\circ = 63^\circ$.

The same argument proves a rule worth remembering: in a zigzag between two parallel lines, the angles opening to the right add up to the same total as the angles opening to the left. Here $38^\circ + x = 74^\circ + 27^\circ$, which gives $x = 63^\circ$ in one line.

Example 2. $ABCDE$ is a regular pentagon, and $ABF$ is an equilateral triangle drawn inside it. Find $\angle CFD$.

The angle we want is in triangle $CFD$, about which we know nothing directly. But there are many equal lengths: the five sides of the pentagon, and $FA = FB = AB$. In particular $BF = BC$, so triangle $BFC$ is isosceles, and this is the step that starts the chase.

The interior angle of the pentagon is $108^\circ$, so $\angle FBC = 108^\circ - 60^\circ = 48^\circ$, and the base angles of triangle $BFC$ are $\angle BFC = \angle BCF = \tfrac12(180^\circ - 48^\circ) = 66^\circ$. Hence $\angle FCD = 108^\circ - 66^\circ = 42^\circ$.

We need one more angle of triangle $CFD$. The whole figure is symmetric about the line through $D$ and the midpoint of $AB$, and $F$ lies on this line because $FA = FB$. So $FD$ bisects $\angle CDE$, giving $\angle FDC = 54^\circ$. Therefore $\angle CFD = 180^\circ - 42^\circ - 54^\circ = 84^\circ$.

We check it another way. By the same isosceles argument $\angle AFE = 66^\circ$, and by symmetry $\angle CFD = \angle DFE$. The angles round $F$ give $60^\circ + 66^\circ + 66^\circ + 2\angle CFD = 360^\circ$, so $\angle CFD = 84^\circ$ again.

Example 3. $ABCD$ is a convex quadrilateral with $AB = AC = AD$. Given that $\angle ACB = 75^\circ$ and $\angle CAD = 64^\circ$, find $\angle BDC$.

Three equal lengths give three isosceles triangles, so a direct chase works. Triangle $ABC$ has $AB = AC$, so $\angle ABC = 75^\circ$ and $\angle BAC = 30^\circ$. Then $\angle BAD = 30^\circ + 64^\circ = 94^\circ$, and the isosceles triangle $ABD$ gives $\angle ADB = \tfrac12(180^\circ - 94^\circ) = 43^\circ$. The isosceles triangle $ACD$ gives $\angle ADC = \tfrac12(180^\circ - 64^\circ) = 58^\circ$. So $\angle BDC = 58^\circ - 43^\circ = 15^\circ$.

Note that the $64^\circ$ cancelled. When a given value does not affect the answer, look for a shorter argument. Since $AB = AC = AD$, the points $B$, $C$, $D$ lie on a circle with centre $A$. The angle $\angle BDC$ stands on the chord $BC$, which subtends $\angle BAC = 30^\circ$ at the centre, and $D$ is on the major arc. So $\angle BDC = 15^\circ$ immediately, and this explains why $D$ could slide anywhere on that arc without changing the answer.

Example 4. $A_1A_2\ldots A_{12}$ is a regular 12-gon. The diagonals $A_1A_5$ and $A_2A_9$ meet at $X$. Find $\angle A_1XA_2$.

Interior angles of $150^\circ$ and isosceles triangles would work, but slowly, especially for $\angle A_1A_2A_9$. Instead, note that all twelve vertices lie on a circle, so every angle between vertices is an angle at the circumference.

Each side subtends $\tfrac{360^\circ}{12} = 30^\circ$ at the centre, so it subtends $15^\circ$ at any other vertex. The angle $\angle A_5A_1A_2$ stands on the arc $A_2A_3A_4A_5$, which contains three sides, so it is $3 \times 15^\circ = 45^\circ$. The angle $\angle A_1A_2A_9$ stands on the arc from $A_9$ through $A_{10}$, $A_{11}$, $A_{12}$ to $A_1$, which contains four sides, so it is $60^\circ$. In triangle $A_1A_2X$ we get $\angle A_1XA_2 = 180^\circ - 45^\circ - 60^\circ = 75^\circ$.

The same argument proves a general fact: two chords crossing inside a circle make an angle equal to half the sum of the central angles of the arcs they cut off, here $\tfrac12(30^\circ + 120^\circ) = 75^\circ$.

Common traps.

  • Trusting the picture. Contest diagrams are often not to scale. Lines are parallel, or a point is the centre, only if you are told so or can prove it.
  • Forgetting the second case. An isosceles triangle with a $40^\circ$ angle could have it at the apex or at the base.
  • Using the centre theorem with the wrong arc. If $C$ is on the minor arc $AB$, it is the reflex angle $AOB$ that equals $2\angle ACB$.
  • Applying "same segment" to points on opposite sides of a chord. Those angles add to $180^\circ$ (a cyclic quadrilateral); they are not equal.
  • Confusing the sum $(n-2)\times 180^\circ$ with a single interior angle, or interior angles with exterior ones.

How to spot this in a contest

If a question gives angles and asks for an angle, it is a chase. Before writing anything, scan for equal lengths (given ones, sides of regular polygons, radii) and mark the isosceles triangles. If the answer seems to need information you do not have, name the unknowns and expect them to cancel, as in the opening problem. If a given number seems irrelevant, or several equal segments leave one point, look for a circle. For regular polygons with many sides, almost always use the circumcircle and the rule of $\tfrac{180^\circ}{n}$ per side. A careful sketch can check an answer, but it never replaces the reasoning.

practice.q: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is seven times each of its exterior angles. How many sides does the polygon have?
practice.hint: At each vertex the interior and exterior angles add to $180^\circ$, and you know what all the exterior angles add to.
practice.sol: Let each exterior angle be $e$. Then each interior angle is $7e$, and since they lie on a straight line, $e + 7e = 180^\circ$, so $e = 22.5^\circ$. The exterior angles of any polygon add to $360^\circ$, so the number of sides is $360 \div 22.5 = 16$.

practice.q: $ABCDEF$ is a regular hexagon and $ABPQR$ is a regular pentagon. They share the side $AB$ and lie on opposite sides of it. Find $\angle AFR$.
practice.hint: Work out the angle $FAR$ first, then look at the lengths $AF$ and $AR$.
practice.sol:
At $A$ the hexagon has interior angle $\angle FAB = 120^\circ$ and the pentagon has interior angle $\angle BAR = 108^\circ$. These two angles lie on opposite sides of $AB$, so the remaining angle round $A$ is $\angle FAR = 360^\circ - 120^\circ - 108^\circ = 132^\circ$.

Both polygons have all their sides equal to $AB$, so $AF = AB = AR$ and triangle $AFR$ is isosceles with apex $A$. Its base angles are $\angle AFR = \angle ARF = \tfrac12(180^\circ - 132^\circ) = 24^\circ$.

practice.q: Point $D$ lies on side $AC$ of triangle $ABC$, and $AB = BD = DC$. Given that $\angle ABC = 102^\circ$, find $\angle BAC$.
practice.hint: Call $\angle ACB = x$ and write every other angle in terms of $x$, using the exterior angle of triangle $BDC$.
practice.sol:
Let $\angle ACB = x$. Since $DB = DC$, triangle $BDC$ is isosceles and $\angle DBC = x$. The angle $\angle BDA$ is an exterior angle of triangle $BDC$, so $\angle BDA = 2x$.

Since $BA = BD$, triangle $ABD$ is isosceles and $\angle BAD = \angle BDA = 2x$, which leaves $\angle ABD = 180^\circ - 4x$. Now $\angle ABC = \angle ABD + \angle DBC = 180^\circ - 3x$. Setting this equal to $102^\circ$ gives $x = 26^\circ$, so $\angle BAC = 2x = 52^\circ$. As a check, the angles of $ABC$ are $52^\circ$, $102^\circ$ and $26^\circ$, which add to $180^\circ$.

practice.q: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral with $AB = AD$ and $\angle BCD = 110^\circ$. Its diagonals meet at $E$, and $\angle AEB = 80^\circ$. Find $\angle CAD$.
practice.hint: Opposite angles of $ABCD$ give $\angle BAD$. Then use the isosceles triangle $ABD$ and angles in the same segment.
practice.sol:
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to $180^\circ$, so $\angle BAD = 70^\circ$. Triangle $ABD$ is isosceles with $AB = AD$, so $\angle ABD = \angle ADB = 55^\circ$.

The angles $\angle ACB$ and $\angle ADB$ stand on the same chord $AB$ on the same side of it, so $\angle ACB = 55^\circ$. In triangle $BEC$ the angle at $E$ is $\angle BEC = 180^\circ - 80^\circ = 100^\circ$, so $\angle EBC = 180^\circ - 100^\circ - 55^\circ = 25^\circ$. That is the angle $\angle DBC$.

Finally $\angle CAD$ and $\angle CBD$ stand on the same chord $CD$, so $\angle CAD = \angle CBD = 25^\circ$.

practice.q: In a regular $n$-gon $A_1A_2A_3\ldots A_n$, the diagonals $A_1A_4$ and $A_2A_6$ meet at $X$, and $\angle A_1XA_2 = 27^\circ$. Find $n$.
practice.hint: Put the polygon in its circumcircle. Each side subtends $\tfrac{180^\circ}{n}$ at any other vertex.
practice.sol:
The vertices lie on a circle, and each side subtends $\tfrac{360^\circ}{n}$ at the centre, hence $\tfrac{180^\circ}{n}$ at any other vertex. The angle $\angle XA_1A_2 = \angle A_4A_1A_2$ stands on the arc $A_2A_3A_4$, which contains $2$ sides, so it equals $2 \times \tfrac{180^\circ}{n}$. The angle $\angle XA_2A_1 = \angle A_6A_2A_1$ stands on the arc from $A_6$ round to $A_1$ that avoids $A_2$, which contains $n - 5$ sides, so it equals $(n-5) \times \tfrac{180^\circ}{n}$.

In triangle $A_1A_2X$, therefore, $\angle A_1XA_2 = 180^\circ - (n-3)\times\tfrac{180^\circ}{n} = \tfrac{540^\circ}{n}$. Setting $\tfrac{540}{n} = 27$ gives $n = 20$. (The diagonals do cross, because $A_2$ lies between $A_1$ and $A_4$ while $A_6$ lies beyond $A_4$.)

practice.q: Seven points $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_7$ lie on a circle in that order, not necessarily equally spaced. Each point is joined to the two points two places away from it round the circle, so $A_1$ is joined to $A_3$ and to $A_6$, and so on. This draws a seven-pointed star. Find the sum of the seven angles at the tips of the star, $\angle A_6A_1A_3 + \angle A_7A_2A_4 + \angle A_1A_3A_5 + \cdots + \angle A_5A_7A_2$.
practice.hint: Each tip angle is an angle at the circumference. Which arc does it stand on, and how many times is each small arc used?
practice.sol:
Let the arcs $A_1A_2, A_2A_3, \ldots, A_7A_1$ (the short arcs between neighbours) subtend angles $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_7$ at the centre, so that $a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_7 = 360^\circ$.

The tip angle $\angle A_6A_1A_3$ is an angle at the circumference standing on the arc from $A_3$ to $A_6$ that avoids $A_1$. That arc is made of the three small arcs $A_3A_4$, $A_4A_5$, $A_5A_6$, so by the angle at the centre theorem $\angle A_6A_1A_3 = \tfrac12(a_3 + a_4 + a_5)$. In the same way, every tip angle is half the sum of three consecutive $a_i$, and as we go round the seven tips each $a_i$ is used in exactly three of them.

So the total is $\tfrac12 \times 3 \times (a_1 + \cdots + a_7) = \tfrac12 \times 3 \times 360^\circ = 540^\circ$. Note that the answer does not depend on where the points are, which is consistent with the regular star, where each tip is $\tfrac{540^\circ}{7}$.
